We present KVCompass, a discovery plane for Internet-scale KV cache sharing. The discovery index supports variable-length prefix lookup with constant-time local table reads at the edge, allowing each request to be forwarded to the worker that best balances KV cache reuse against load and network distance. Evaluation includes a 64-worker geo-distributed simulation and a 14-worker three-continent real-machine testbed. Evaluation shows that KVCompass achieves $1.3-14\times$ lower P99 TTFT than the baselines, up to $3.7\times$ lower P99 end-to-end latency, up to $4.7\times$ the throughput, and a peak load factor within 2% of the Oracle floor.

# LoopHIL: Looping Hardware into LLM-assisted Agents for Wireless Embedded Systems LLM agents are widely used for software development and debugging, but their adoption in embedded systems, especially for wireless tasks, remains limited. This is because embedded development requires hardware-in-the-loop testing. Agents cannot directly observe the spectrum, probe pins, or measure power, so they cannot verify wireless link functionality; currently, human engineers perform this verification. We systematically evaluate whether LLM agents can establish wireless links when provided with hardware access. We introduce LoopHIL, a framework that lets agents control a multi-device RF bench, monitor it with a spectrum analyzer, logic analyzer, and energy meter, and validate links against a verification ladder, all within code-enforced safety limits. Across four increasingly complex tasks, from generating a carrier to backscatter decoding by a commercial receiver, and using six models from two vendors, hardware-in-the-loop increases task completion rates from 54% to 79% and from 17% to 83% on the most challenging task. It also halves task time and output tokens. With debugging tools, agents decrease tag power consumption by up to 96%. However, small models often report unverified claims, so independent hardware checks remain necessary.

# Who Plans, Who Edits? Verified, Cost-Aware Division of Labor for LLM-Driven Analog Layout Repair Language-model agents can repair analog layouts when sign-off tools check every edit, but which model should plan a repair, which should edit it, and at what cost remain open questions. In our tool-grounded repair agent, models only choose bounded layout operators; sign-off tools rerun each task's contract checks after every edit, so failing layouts are never accepted. On layout-versus-schematic (LVS), design-rule checking (DRC), and post-layout repairs of three designs (a production high-voltage digital-to-analog converter (DAC), a 5-V oscillator, and a SKY130 operational transconductance amplifier (OTA)) with six tier-matched models from two vendors, 182 blind runs show that cheap models execute plans but rarely succeed alone (the cheapest model: 1 of 11 runs alone, 16 of 17 under a flagship planner; p < 0.001), cheap planners fail more often, and no fixed assignment is cheapest on every task.

On layout-versus-schematic (LVS), design-rule checking (DRC), and post-layout repairs of three designs (a production high-voltage digital-to-analog converter (DAC), a 5-V oscillator, and a SKY130 operational transconductance amplifier (OTA)) with six tier-matched models from two vendors, 182 blind runs show that cheap models execute plans but rarely succeed alone (the cheapest model: 1 of 11 runs alone, 16 of 17 under a flagship planner; p < 0.001), cheap planners fail more often, and no fixed assignment is cheapest on every task. We propose a learning controller that selects models for each role and the escalation order from the first tool evaluation and updates Bayesian estimates after every attempt. With rules and initial estimates frozen before testing, the controller fixed 7 of 8 episodes on four sealed held-out tasks, matching the OpenAI flagship alone, at 15-40% of the flagship's spend per fix on three tasks but 8% higher spend overall. The cheapest mid-tier model alone fixed 6 of 8 at the lowest overall spend per fix but missed the hardest task.

The cheapest mid-tier model alone fixed 6 of 8 at the lowest overall spend per fix but missed the hardest task. All 32 extracted DAC repairs match the human-guided LVS repair's integral nonlinearity (INL) within 0.005 least significant bits (LSB) at every code.

# Empirical Analysis of TEE-Enabled Rollup Designs Layer 2 (L2) rollups have become the dominant scaling solution in Ethereum. At the core of these systems lies the rollup sequencer, a component that orders, executes, and submits L2 transaction blocks to the main Ethereum blockchain. The centralization of this sequencer introduces security risks, including censorship and malicious manipulation of transactions to extract maximum extractable value (MEV). Trusted execution environments (TEEs) provide strong hardware-enforced confidentiality and integrity guarantees for code and data. TEEs are strong candidates for strengthening security and ensuring verifiable neutrality in rollup sequencer operations, but multiple TEE-based designs are possible, offering different trade-offs among modularity, performance, and security guarantees. Among them, the separation of proposer and builder logic (PBS) into independent services is a strong contender against the monolithic approach that bundles all sequencer logic. Despite several proposed theoretical frameworks, there is a lack of experimental evaluation of the practicality and security trade-offs of integrating TEEs into rollup sequencers.

Despite several proposed theoretical frameworks, there is a lack of experimental evaluation of the practicality and security trade-offs of integrating TEEs into rollup sequencers. This work addresses this gap through a comprehensive empirical study of TEE-enabled rollup designs under both PBS and monolithic sequencer models. Our experimental evaluations show that the impact of TEEs on rollup performance is small and that PBS does not significantly amplify it. We also show that PBS can lead to significant performance improvements by enabling more specialized, efficient builder logic implementations.

# MAC units for a 2x2 int8 systolic array on Tiny Tapeout We take the multiply-accumulate (MAC) unit of an open-source 2$\times$2 int8 systolic array taped out on Tiny Tapeout (GF180 process) and propose two replacements. The first one, \emph{hybrid}, uses a different arithmetic structure for each row of the array. It reduces the logic area of one MAC unit by 4--6\% and of the whole chip by 0.7--3.2\% after place and route. The second one, \emph{fused\_eq}, never builds the long carry chain of the accumulation. It shortens the critical path by 20\% for one MAC unit and by 14\% for the whole chip. All numbers come from the standard Tiny Tapeout flow (LibreLane) run in GitHub Actions. Correctness is checked by exhaustive simulation of all $2^{24}$ inputs, a formal equivalence proof, and the original test bench.

# SigmaTrace: Library-Agnostic Observability for CPU/GPU-Initiated RDMA Communication RDMA networking enables low-latency, high-bandwidth communication on large systems. Despite its adoption, however, observability is lacking. Existing tools target specific communication libraries or only report aggregated data, missing per-operation behavior. The gap is widest for GPU-initiated networking, whose in-kernel RDMA operations are invisible to the host. We present SigmaTrace, a library-agnostic RDMA profiling framework providing fine-grained, per-operation visibility for CPU and GPU-initiated networking. It traces operations at the libibverbs/mlx5dv layers, the common denominator beneath communication libraries on InfiniBand and RoCE, and employs a low-overhead memory interposition technique that, to our knowledge, gives the first observability into GPU-initiated RDMA without source patching or binary instrumentation. Host-side tracing adds 1.3% overhead on NCCL AllReduce at 128 GPUs and under 2% on RCCL at 1024 GPUs. On a persistent-kernel BFS and Mixture-of-Experts inference, SigmaTrace exposes an in-kernel barrier spread and 2.13x inter-node traffic skew invisible to existing profilers.

# FTWeave: Composing Logical Execution, Real-Time Decoding, and Magic-State Supply in Tightly Integrated Quantum-Classical Systems Fault-tolerant quantum applications depend on both decoded measurement information and a continuing supply of magic states. While an operation waits for either, its logical data require protection that produces more syndrome data and decoding work. Architects must provision the quantum and classical parts of the machine together, before complete systems are available to measure. FTWeave is a system-level simulator for this architectural exploration. It accepts OpenQASM 2/3 circuits, CUDA-Q Logical compiler artifacts, Stim circuits, and provider-derived physical inputs through adapters that preserve operation and measurement dependencies. Users bind these inputs to quantum resources, classical processors, memory, communication, and factory configurations. One event timeline determines application progress, resource ownership, and continuing protection. This supplies the system model needed to connect circuit and decoder evidence to application performance. Controlled demand studies and complete multiplier and Ising circuits show why the coupling changes provisioning decisions.

Controlled demand studies and complete multiplier and Ising circuits show why the coupling changes provisioning decisions. A fixed-work approximation predicts a 3.55x multiplier speedup from additional factories where the coupled model gives almost none. Explicit ownership also changes useful capacity: increasing decoder workers alone has no benefit in a storage-constrained case, while increasing workers and feedback entries together gives 4.93x speedup. Selected color and hypergraph-product code mappings take 53-90% longer under decoder service variability, despite an unchanged mean. These comparisons identify useful resource combinations and distinguish protection work from the elapsed lifetime of quantum data.

# Koi: Evidence-Guided, Self-Calibrating Planning for Multi-Cloud, Heterogeneous LLM Inference Fleets Deploying a large language model (LLM) requires choosing the right accelerator, parallelization strategy, engine configuration, and replica count amongst ~140 other variables across clouds, regions, and markets. These decisions are intertwined, and the best cluster-wide plan continually changes as jobs contend for shared capacity on shifting workloads. We present Koi, a self-calibrating cluster planner for heterogeneous, multi-cloud fleets. Koi uses a Recursive Language Model (RLM) hierarchy to propose hypotheses and reason over deployment while deterministic components predict serving behavior, score candidates, and control placement. It represents inference behavior as a fixed causal graph linking decisions (e.g., accelerator, parallelism), runtime mediators (e.g., KV-cache pressure, communication overhead), and outcomes (e.g., latency, throughput). Each deployment strengthens or weakens scoped causal relationships, building a comprehensive playbook for inference that the planner employs to guide future decisions. Job-wise configurations are composed into cluster-wide plans and evaluated against serving objectives, resource constraints, SLO risks, and cost. Across benchmarks, Koi achieves 1.18x greater goodput than the strongest baseline while reducing $/token by 20% in a real heterogeneous cluster. Ablations isolate the contribution of Koi's architecture: a pure language model attains a composite score of 35.3, the same model equipped with Koi's deterministic tools reaches 51.6, and the full Koi planner reaches 70.8.

# Adding Heavy-Ball Momentum to Distributed Constrained Optimization for Energy Resource Management Subject to Time-Delays and Quantization This paper studies a hybrid discrete-time signed gradient-consensus method with heavy-ball momentum, paired communication delays, and fixed logarithmic quantization. The method preserves the aggregate supply-demand equality at every iteration. For a static connected undirected graph and bounded delays, a Lyapunov-Krasovskii analysis establishes practical stability by isolating the discontinuous quantization error as an additive disturbance and closing a computable invariant-sublevel argument. The resulting ergodic residual bound is quadratic in the quantization resolution, and exact convergence to the smooth penalized equality-constrained optimizer is recovered in the unquantized case. For delay-free unquantized quadratic costs, an exact modal analysis identifies the heavy-ball stability region and optimal parameters, with the predicted rate validated on a fixed sparse network. A reproducible delayed experiment reports all constants and a certificate whose guaranteed steady-state level lies below the reported initialization. A separate mixed generator-battery experiment exercises the signed update directly. Finite smooth penalties approximate, but do not generally enforce, the local box constraints exactly.

# Low-Bit Distributed Constrained Optimization with Application to Optimal Scheduling and Allocation This paper proposes a distributed resource allocation algorithm in which each agent communicates only the sign of its local cost gradient, a single bit per directed link per iteration. The algorithm is based on Laplacian-gradient dynamics and preserves the equality (demand) constraint at every iterate, guaranteeing anytime feasibility irrespective of termination time. First, we provide a complete Lyapunov-based convergence analysis for the fixed-step-size regime: the iterates are shown to enter, in at most O(1/\varepsilon^2) iterations, a neighborhood of the optimizer whose radius scales as O(τ) in the decision variable and O(τ^2) in the cost residual, where $τ$ is the step-size. Crucially, the step-size bound is a time-invariant network constant (depending only on the graph Laplacian spectrum and the cost curvature bounds), so no adaptive tuning is required.

Crucially, the step-size bound is a time-invariant network constant (depending only on the graph Laplacian spectrum and the cost curvature bounds), so no adaptive tuning is required. Second, we characterize the invariant set under B-connected, weight-balanced digraphs, strictly weaker than the all-time connectivity and doubly-stochastic weights assumed in most prior work, and show that any odd, sign-preserving nonlinearity yields the same invariant-set and descent structure, with the single-bit protocol being the extreme communication-minimizing instance of a broader nonlinear class. Third, we address local box constraints via smooth penalty relaxation and quantify explicitly how the penalty weight interacts with the step-size bound and the optimality gap. Simulations on economic dispatch (1000 generators) and CPU scheduling (500 servers) demonstrate that the single-bit protocol achieves 5-60 times reduction in total communication cost relative to multi-bit baselines, at the price of a tunable and explicitly bounded optimality gap. A diminishing step-size schedule is shown empirically to eliminate this gap; its formal convergence analysis is identified as an open problem.

# SENTRY: A Streaming Edge Network Trust Engine for Real-Time Audio Deepfake Detection Real-time voice cloning has enabled large-scale streaming deepfake and vishing attacks, while existing Network Detection and Response (NDR) solutions rely on GPU-based post-processing that requires buffered audio and generalizes poorly to unseen speech synthesis models. This paper presents SENTRY, a hardware-oriented, streaming trust engine for inline deepfake detection at the network edge. SENTRY employs an integer lifting-wavelet front end together with a bank of multiplier-free transforms, including wavelet-packet envelopes, Walsh-Hadamard sequency profiles, waveform micro-statistics, and long-term spectral features, designed so that acoustic analysis needs only integer add, shift, compare and bitwise operations. A supervised gradient-boosted tree classifier is combined with an unsupervised Mahalanobis out-of-distribution detector trained solely on authentic speech, and their outputs are fused by a lightweight logistic layer to produce graduated LOG, CHALLENGE, or DROP actions.

A supervised gradient-boosted tree classifier is combined with an unsupervised Mahalanobis out-of-distribution detector trained solely on authentic speech, and their outputs are fused by a lightweight logistic layer to produce graduated LOG, CHALLENGE, or DROP actions. Under a closed-set protocol, SENTRY reaches 98.75% accuracy at a 1.25% equal-error rate (EER) on WaveFake, with perfect separation of HiFi-GAN and WaveGlow; its supervised track alone achieves an AUC of 0.9994 (fused: 0.9993). On ASVspoof 2019 LA (attacks A01-A06) over an 8 kHz mu-law telephony channel, it reaches 94.75% accuracy at a 5.05% EER, with a supervised-track AUC of 0.9948 (fused: 0.9884) and per-attack EERs below 7%. In our prototype, the feature front end runs as bit-exact integer code on one Arm Cortex-A53 core, and the classifier and fusion stage are synthesized for a Xilinx Zynq UltraScale+ MPSoC using no DSP slices, returning a decision 220 ns after a feature vector is ready.

In our prototype, the feature front end runs as bit-exact integer code on one Arm Cortex-A53 core, and the classifier and fusion stage are synthesized for a Xilinx Zynq UltraScale+ MPSoC using no DSP slices, returning a decision 220 ns after a feature vector is ready. These results indicate that deepfake screening can be placed inline without GPUs or floating-point hardware; generalization to unseen generators is left to future work.

# TideKV: Delayed KV Eviction via Layer-Wise Chunked Prefill for Memory-Efficient Long-Context LLM Inference Long-context large language model (LLM) inference is important for modern intelligent applications but remains constrained by peak memory during prompt prefill. Existing KV cache compression reduces decoding memory but typically requires full-prompt prefill to preserve global context, retaining a high construction peak. Online chunk-level eviction lowers memory earlier but selects before each layer has observed the complete prompt, potentially degrading cache construction and decoding. We present TideKV, an on-GPU cache-construction architecture using layer-major delayed eviction. TideKV processes all prompt chunks within each Transformer layer, retains full-prompt KV only for the active layer, and evicts at layer end. This schedule preserves full-prompt-aware selection while reducing activation and temporary memory. Experiments across multiple computing platforms show that TideKV preserves the inference quality and final cache size of the evaluated compression methods. At 64K on A100, it reduces the construction-time transient footprint by 83.89%. On RTX 4090, it increases time to first token by only 1.06% at 64K and enables 128K prefill. TideKV also completes 128K on Jetson, whereas matched post-prefill compression runs out of memory on both resource-constrained platforms. These results show that delayed layer-end eviction substantially expands feasible context lengths without sacrificing cache utility.

# Discrete Phase-Shift Optimization of Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces using Uniform Reference Directions Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (RISs) enable programmable control of the wireless propagation environment through adjustable reflecting elements. A fundamental challenge in RIS-assisted communications is the optimization of discrete phase shifts to maximize the received signal power. While recently developed algorithms can obtain optimal solutions with linear complexity, their computational cost may still be excessive in applications requiring large-scale simulations, real-time adaptation, or repeated optimization over numerous channel realizations. This paper proposes a low-complexity discrete phase-shift optimization algorithm based on multiple reference directions within the feasible optimality sector. By evaluating candidate phase configurations generated from uniformly distributed reference directions, the proposed method systematically improves upon existing approximation approaches that rely on a fixed set of reference directions. The number of reference directions serves as a design parameter that enables a controllable trade-off between computational complexity and optimality. Extensive simulations demonstrate that the proposed algorithm achieves substantial computational speedups while maintaining a small optimality gap relative to the optimal solution. The results further show that increasing the number of reference directions progressively reduces the optimality gap, providing flexible operating points that can be tailored to application-specific complexity and performance requirements.

# SpikeDuet: CPU-Accelerator Co-Execution of Sparse SNNs on Commodity MCUs Spiking neural networks (SNNs) expose sparse event activity, but commodity microcontrollers increasingly pair general-purpose processors with dense matrix-vector accelerators whose suitability for sparse inference is unclear. We investigate whether the on-chip Matrix Vector Processor (MVP) of the EFR32MG24 can accelerate SNN inference beyond optimized event-driven Cortex-M33 execution. Our automated snnTorch-to-C deployment flow combines hardware-calibrated engine selection, function-preserving neuron reordering that places co-active neurons adjacently for the accelerator, and asynchronous scheduling that overlaps CPU and MVP computation. On physical hardware, heterogeneous execution achieves 1.27--1.87$\times$ speedup and 11--34\% lower energy per inference than optimized sparse Cortex-M33 execution across five evaluated network configurations, while the smallest Braille network remains CPU-optimal. Reordering alone moves Braille-384's dominant hidden layer from the CPU to the MVP, and its benefit persists under asynchronous execution. These results show that activity locality and concurrency between CPU and MVP can jointly improve sparse SNN inference on commodity MCUs.

# Heart Signal (ECG) as Vibration Signature for Human Authentication Using TinyML Ensuring data security in the era of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and deepfake technology requires robust biometric systems. Conventional methods such as facial recognition, iris scans, fingerprints, and voice recognition are increasingly vulnerable to spoofing and provide only one-time authentication at login. This study introduces an Electrocardiogram (ECG) based authentication framework, compared with Photoplethysmography (PPG), leveraging Tiny Machine Learning (TinyML) for deployment on resource-constrained microcontroller units (MCUs). The proposed method enables continuous authentication, offering ongoing verification throughout device usage, which conventional biometrics cannot achieve. It also serves as a password-free solution, reducing risks of credential loss, theft, or reuse. However, ECG signals vary with physical activity, health conditions, age, and emotional states, requiring robust signal processing and learning algorithms. To address this, efficient TinyML models were designed to mitigate recognition errors from noisy real-time data. Experiments used single-lead ECG signals (Lead I) from UofTDB, MIT-BIH Arrhythmia, MIT-BIH Noise Stress Test, and PTB databases.

Experiments used single-lead ECG signals (Lead I) from UofTDB, MIT-BIH Arrhythmia, MIT-BIH Noise Stress Test, and PTB databases. Spectrograms and spectral features were extracted to train Deep Neural Network (DNN), 1D CNN, and 2D CNN models within the Edge Impulse platform, achieving 98% accuracy. The trained model was converted into TinyML format and deployed on an Espressif ESP-EYE (ESP32, 240 MHz). Support Vector Machine (SVM) models were also applied for benchmarking. By analyzing the number of heartbeats required for reliable recognition, the results show that averaging multiple signals improves tolerance to noise and enhances accuracy. Overall, ECG-based authentication demonstrates strong potential as a secure, real-time, and continuously verifiable method for personal identification on wearable and edge devices.

# HEL: A Heterogeneous Extensible Layer for GPU-Resident Runtime Orchestration We describe a GPU-resident runtime system, HEL, built on stateful services that persist throughout the lifespan of a user application. A HEL programmer expresses a workload as an application that spawns coroutine-like tasks, which are then scheduled and run by the HEL runtime. HEL supports synchronous and asynchronous tasks, tasks with runtime dependencies, batched task submission, and automatic retries. Applications and tasks run alongside each other on the spatially partitioned GPU. Using producer-consumer and host-RPC benchmarks together with a PFPL compression case study, we show that HEL demonstrates a performance advantage for underutilized GPUs and for scenarios where HEL enables hiding task latency.

# A mechanism for collective foraging: percolating recruitment cascades coupled to a maximum-entropy field Foraging recruitment is a contagion: an agent that finds a resource triggers a linear-threshold cascade, the model built for rumour and adoption spread on social networks, now embedded in space. Because activation is degree-normalized, the same rule that spreads the cascade also stifles it as neighbourhoods crowd, so the swarm aggregates on a resource and then releases to explore again. The cascade runs on the communication network, but acting on it moves agents in physical space, and that motion rewires the network: network and space are one coupled system, and this feedback, not any tuning, makes the coordination self-limiting. Because recruitment chains along the graph rather than reaching near neighbours alone, whether a discovery stays local or spans the swarm is a question of percolation. The swarm holds itself in a cascade window that is locally near-critical though globally subcritical, a self-organized, self-limiting drive-release cycle, sandpile-like but non-conservative.

The swarm holds itself in a cascade window that is locally near-critical though globally subcritical, a self-organized, self-limiting drive-release cycle, sandpile-like but non-conservative. Nothing is tuned, yet behaviours that foraging biology documents separately emerge together: recruitment to discoveries, marginal-value patch-leaving, and Levy search with a switch to local exploitation. These follow from one least-committal principle, the resource field and the search both as maximum entropy, with Levy search matched to the field's sparsity and recruitment to its clustering, so active-matter order and optimal foraging appear as one system seen in two domains. The gains are real but conditional: up to 7.6x the harvest of solitary search when resources are sparse and clustered, shrinking to nothing when search is already easy. That sparse, clustered field is also the generic one, because resources almost inevitably aggregate, so one untuned rule should recur widely.

# BitPCE: Batched Multi-Dimensional PolicyResolution with GPU Bitmap Algebra Policy controllers must determine which workloads match rules spanning several label dimensions. Hash sets, compressed bitmaps, and GPU set-processing primitives address the underlying set operations. However, intermediate results, repeated scope evaluations, dependent policy updates, and host transfers can dominate the cost of a heterogeneous batch. We study this problem as batched intersection-of-unions (IoU). Our design exploits independent scope--word tasks, reusable endpoint expressions, and policy dependencies. The challenges are preserving wildcard, empty-group, and exclusion semantics, recognizing equal scopes, and retaining unchanged recipients affected by source edits. BitPCE addresses them with register-resident GPU evaluation, canonical scope compilation, and dependency-complete candidate selection under a stated rendering contract. IP-only changes reuse cached memberships. We establish correctness and word-work bounds. On a four-vCPU A10G host, resident GPU execution is 3.46--36.60$\times$ faster than the best tested native CPU path, including CRoaring, and 1.14--2.22$\times$ faster than an adapted operand-parallel GPU reduction. Gains narrow at the host-output boundary: on an eight-vCPU host, including upload and compact identifier output, resolution takes 16.3 ms versus 19.3 ms for CPU at 100K objects and 500 scopes. Sparse labels and small batches can favor CPU execution. Scope reuse, candidate selection, and incremental transfers are measured as components; complete update-to-enforcement latency remains unevaluated.

# Hierarchical Rule Auditing with Exact Ternary GPU Correlation Auditing firewall logs against requirements mapped to controls and frameworks must retain overlapping obligations, preserve uncertainty from missing attributes and count distinct affected records. Direct, bitmap and relational methods can express this audit; a correlation implementation must preserve distinctions that ordinary match counts and rule-hit totals discard. We present an exact ternary correlation algorithm that compiles categorical conjunctions into one bounded-integer matrix product. A dominating false-predicate penalty separates known mismatches from missing evidence, while per-record hierarchy unions prevent duplicate counting. We prove their composition and handle high-cardinality endpoints through exact address classes and versioned labels. Evaluation compares eight CPU/GPU implementations, includes public traffic and 133 published source-address ACLs with generated observations, and measures hierarchy and policy-rebuild costs. On an NVIDIA L4, matched fused execution reduces latency by 8.8 to 11.2 percent relative to two-product correlation across five tested shapes. At 100,000 records and 1,024 requirements, it takes 12.28 ms versus 13.82 ms for two products and 12.29 ms for GPU bitmaps. Bitmaps remain faster in most regimes, with hierarchy operations and reductions dominating the measured fused-correlation stage intervals.

# Conjugate Compilation: Self-Improving Agentic Co-Compilation for Speculative Decoding As LLM adoption surges, scaling model serving requires unlocking stranded GPU capacity alongside deploying more GPUs. Speculative decoding brings two models into the serving process: a small draft model proposes tokens that a larger target model verifies. Yet compiling these models individually leaves their shared execution outside the compiler's optimization boundary. We introduce CONJUGATE COMPILATION, which reframes speculative decoding as a cross-model compilation problem and jointly optimizes the draft and target models within their shared execution rather than treating each in isolation. Our key insight is that cross-model compilation should be informed by the measured performance of the co-located shared execution it produces: an optimization that improves a kernel in isolation need not improve the models when they execute together. To expand cross-model opportunities, we devise operand layouts that interleave blocks from both models within common tiles, co-locating GEMM and non-GEMM work while preserving their mathematics.

To expand cross-model opportunities, we devise operand layouts that interleave blocks from both models within common tiles, co-locating GEMM and non-GEMM work while preserving their mathematics. We realize CONJUGATE COMPILATION through a self-improving agentic search system in which an LLM edits cross-model optimization plans using the compiler and GPU execution as its environment. Each proposed plan is compiled and evaluated through its co-located shared execution, whose measured score, together with kernel-level verdicts and compiler feedback, informs subsequent proposals, while Monte Carlo tree search accumulates rewards to guide exploration. Across six single-GPU speculative-decoding configurations on NVIDIA B300 and RTX 5090 GPUs, CONJUGATE COMPILATION achieves a geometric-mean per-round speedup of 1.37x over conventional execution. Interleaved kernels raise this speedup to 1.45x, reaching 1.59x in the best case. CONJUGATE COMPILATION also improves GPU utilization on average by 1.46x on RTX 5090 and 1.50x on B300.

# PlaneZip: Lossless Bit-Plane Compression of Training Activations Offloaded over PCIe Training under a device-memory budget relies on tensor rematerialization: an evicted activation is either swapped to host memory or dropped and recomputed. Because GPU compute has outgrown PCIe bandwidth, cost-model planners such as MegTaiChi, which charge a swap its full transfer time, almost never swap, and swaps that fill idle link time carry only a small fraction of the saved activations. Saved activations, however, are homogeneously typed arrays with bit-level redundancy beyond zeros, which lightweight bit-plane compressors can remove at line rate. We present PlaneZip, which compresses swapped tensors on the copy path and plans around the compression. Its codec picks, for every 128-byte block, the smallest of zero-value, delta bit-plane, bit-plane, and a new zero-masked bit-plane encoding. A per-tensor predictor reuses the ratio of the previous iteration, and the planner budgets link time in compressed transfer times.

A per-tensor predictor reuses the ratio of the previous iteration, and the planner budgets link time in compressed transfer times. On activations captured from five models trained on real data, the codec compresses BF16 activations by 1.71x and FP32 activations by 1.39x (geometric means), against 1.18x and 1.20x for zero-value compression. In trace-driven simulation of a PCIe 3.0 consumer GPU and a PCIe 4.0 datacenter GPU at half the activation memory, PlaneZip cuts the rematerialization overhead by 47% and 31% relative to a bandwidth-aware planner without compression, and by 73% and 54% relative to MegTaiChi's cost model, with an estimated engine area of 0.036 square millimeters.

# Mixed-Precision GPU Acceleration for Confidence Regions of Spatial Excursion Sets A spatial excursion set identifies where a field exceeds a threshold. With incomplete and noisy observations, inner and outer confidence regions quantify uncertainty in its spatial extent through lower and upper bounds at a specified confidence level. Constructing these regions requires repeated conditional simulations accounting for joint spatial uncertainty, making dense covariance factorization and simulation major computational bottlenecks. We present a GPU-accelerated framework that combines adaptive tile-based mixed-precision arithmetic with distributed task execution to accelerate universal kriging, prediction-uncertainty estimation, conditional Gaussian simulation, and confidence region calibration. In our parallel mixed-precision simulation workflow, triangular matrix-matrix multiplication (TRMM) inherits the adaptive precision layout of the Cholesky factor and uses FP16 simulation operands, while covariance scaling and compensating operand rescaling accommodate the numerical range of reduced precision arithmetic. With appropriate precision tolerances, empirical coverage is close to the double-precision reference and the nominal 90% confidence level across weak, medium, and strong spatial correlation.

With appropriate precision tolerances, empirical coverage is close to the double-precision reference and the nominal 90% confidence level across weak, medium, and strong spatial correlation. Ocean surface-salinity experiments show close agreement with the double-precision reference in spatial predictions and confidence regions. On four NVIDIA A100 GPUs (40 GB each), mixed-precision TRMM reaches 6.36x to 6.93x the theoretical FP64 peak throughput. On four NVIDIA GH200 Hopper GPUs, it reaches 10.20x to 11.03x. Each AMD MI250X node has eight GPU dies. Aggregate throughput rises by 9.1x to 11.5x from 1 to 16 nodes under weak scaling and by 1.6x to 1.9x from 4 to 16 nodes under strong scaling. Adaptive mixed-precision accelerates large-scale excursion set analysis while preserving the statistical accuracy required for spatial uncertainty quantification.

# Triple Overlap in Pipelined Krylov Methods on Multi-GPU Systems We introduce a novel triple-overlap implementation of the pipelined preconditioned conjugate gradient (Pipe-PCG) and pipelined stabilized biconjugate gradient (Pipe-BiCGStab) solvers, methods widely used in scientific applications. By leveraging a collective communication library, our approach extends conventional computation-communication overlap to concurrently execute collective operations, irregular P2P communication, and compute kernels, enabling computation-communication-communication overlap across multiple GPUs. We evaluate the design on the MareNostrum 5 (H100) and Leonardo (A100) supercomputers, comparing against PETSc and the state-of-the-art two-stream NCCL implementation using SuiteSparse matrices and three massive instances scaled up to 512 GPUs. The three-stream design outperforms the two-stream baseline on every instance, with the margin widening from 2-6% at 4 GPUs to 18-47% at 64 GPUs. At 64 GPUs, the geometric-mean speedup over the two-stream baseline is 1.33x on MareNostrum 5 and 1.23x on Leonardo for Pipe-PCG, and reaches 1.30x for Pipe-BiCGStab. In large-scale experiments, we observed a speedup up to 35% in Pipe-PCG and up to 33% in Pipe-BiCGStab compared to the two-stream design. For PETSc, the margin is even wider, up to 3.27x speedup in both Pipe-PCG and Pipe-BiCGStab. Related code for the proposed method is available online: https://github.com/ParCoreLab/aCG

# Ineffective Occupancy in Heterogeneous GPU Clusters: Prediction, Contribution Analysis, and Readiness-Aware Scheduling In heterogeneous GPU clusters, GPUs are costly and scarce, yet placing a job on a machine does not mean that the job becomes ready to run. A large amount of allocated capacity can remain occupied for long periods without producing useful computation, further aggravating the waste of compute resources. On the Alibaba GPU cluster trace we find that, even when GPU capacity is sufficient and placement is complete, 52.70% of execution records never became ready. We term this phenomenon ineffective occupancy. Building on this diagnosis, and keeping the placement policy fixed, we propose Readiness-Aware Scheduling (RAS): it uses only nine attributes observable at admission time to predict readiness probability and reorders admission accordingly. Under a five-fold split grouped by machine, the gradient-boosted model reaches an ROC-AUC of 0.8187.

Under a five-fold split grouped by machine, the gradient-boosted model reaches an ROC-AUC of 0.8187. A feature-group contribution analysis shows that the model's score is driven mainly by job profile, duration, and GPU model, with the request-size group contributing least, followed by the scheduling and concurrency group. In GPU terms, RAS reduces the ineffective-occupancy ratio (the share of cluster GPUs held under ineffective occupancy) from 43.64% to 27.15% and raises the effective coverage of large requests (eight GPUs or more) from 46.11% to 63.18%, without sacrificing capacity utilization. Relative to the upper bound obtained by ordering with ground-truth labels, RAS captures 65.1% of the attainable improvement, well above the interpretable rules built only from the contribution-analysis conclusions; the gain therefore comes mainly from predicting with all nine attributes jointly rather than from combining rules built on any single attribute group. These results indicate that readiness status is a measurable, predictable, and optimizable dimension of admission decisions in heterogeneous GPU clusters.

# Visual Cache Reuse for Efficient Multimodal Inference Vision-language model (VLM) inference incurs substantial prefill latency and memory overhead due to the long visual token sequences of large visual inputs. Existing serving systems typically exploit exact cache reuse through prefix caching or position-independent caching, overlooking the potential of approximate caching in real-world workloads. However, directly reusing an approximate cache entry may introduce spurious visual information, which naive approaches that select a subset of important visual tokens for recomputation fail to adequately mitigate this risk. We present VisMemo, an efficient serving system that enables approximate KV cache reuse for modern VLMs. Its core is a system-algorithm co-design that combines an entropy-aware KV cache reuse algorithm with differentiated cache management. Specifically, VisMemo uses patch entropy to identify reuse candidates and warmup attention to prioritize recomputation based on the current query.

Specifically, VisMemo uses patch entropy to identify reuse candidates and warmup attention to prioritize recomputation based on the current query. To support the large cache capacity across GPU memory, CPU memory, and SSD storage, VisMemo applies distinct I/O and cache policies to exact and approximate hits: sparse patch-level I/O for approximate hits, prioritized retention for exact hits, and a reserved CPU victim cache for preset entries selected using offline workload priors and online reuse observations. VisMemo further optimizes the memory access path between the inference engine and the storage backend, eliminating redundant caching and unnecessary data movement. Experiments on multiple public datasets show that VisMemo preserves output quality under approximate reuse. On a real-world production trace, VisMemo increases the overall cache hit rate from 27.78% to 61.45% and reduces prefill latency by up to 48.3% at 8K input tokens.

# Off-Tree Forwarding for Accelerating Broadcasts from Arbitrary Sources in Plumtree Overlay broadcast is fundamental to large-scale distributed systems, enabling messages to be disseminated to all participants. Plumtree is a well-established protocol that embeds a spanning tree in a gossip overlay: payloads are disseminated along tree links, while non-tree links support recovery and optimization. However, because the tree is constructed from the first broadcast, it is optimized for the initial source and can introduce long detours for broadcasts originating at other nodes, particularly leaf nodes. To address this limitation, we propose probabilistic exuding, an off-tree forwarding mechanism in which nodes near the source additionally forward payloads over their non-tree links with a specified probability. Exuded messages use a dedicated message type and do not participate in tree construction or repair, leaving the shared tree unchanged. Simulations on a 1000-node random regular overlay show that, for randomly selected sources and a representative parameter setting, the proposed method reduces the 95th-percentile delivery latency by approximately 40% relative to Plumtree.

Simulations on a 1000-node random regular overlay show that, for randomly selected sources and a representative parameter setting, the proposed method reduces the 95th-percentile delivery latency by approximately 40% relative to Plumtree. This closes approximately 92% of the latency gap between Plumtree and flooding while sending only about 58% as many payload messages as flooding. In contrast, Plumtree's own link optimization and shorter repair timeouts, which also exploit non-tree links, rewire the shared tree and increase latency as broadcast sources change; the latency of exuding is nearly unaffected.

# panvram: GPU-resident random access to a human pangenome cohort Repeatedly sampling short sequence windows from a human pangenome requires an access representation as well as compression. panvram stores each assembly as a reference-relative block archive and pools these archives on a GPU. For 558 haplotype assemblies, the default q4k representation occupies 16.642 GB of persistent pools including the decoded reference; a packed-reference, compact-directory representation occupies 11.634 GB. These quantities are not peak application memory. In the C1 experiment, default and fully compact forms delivered 743,271 and 736,762 windows/s; a separate public Colab run delivered 741,931 and 680,760 windows/s. All are batch API measurements and must not be pooled as repeated trials of an identical environment. Full-decoding checks compared reconstructed FASTA checksums with the manifest. On the CPU, the M6 shuffled-window workload at the same cohort cardinality reported 26 requests/s for AGC and 145,222 requests/s for refrel3 q4k. This comparison concerns one-thread requests of 4 KiB on the recorded warm-cache workload, not all genome-access patterns.

This comparison concerns one-thread requests of 4 KiB on the recorded warm-cache workload, not all genome-access patterns. AGC provides the smaller incremental archive: 5.40 MB/assembly versus 13.04 MB/assembly for refrel3 q16k, with different exclusions; the size pair is not the same refrel3 configuration as the q4k timing pair. We derive an expected-work expression for fixed independent granules and distinguish it from an empirical median-latency predictor. Cohort-scale counter and DRAM measurements motivate a locality hypothesis, but do not establish a causal per-miss latency or independently reproduce a model-failure verdict. The window-cost verdict at N=558 is published with its harness and raw timings.

# An Information-Geometric Framework for OCS-Reconfigurable Interconnect Topology in Large-Scale AI Clusters Optical Circuit Switches (OCS) make inter-pod wiring in AI clusters programmable, posing design questions on wiring choice, symmetry departure, and reconfigurations. We present a unified information-geometric framework to address these issues.A wiring is a point in a probability simplex over circuits within a degree polytope. Departure from a symmetric Fat-Tree prior $\mathbf{q}$ is measured by $\DKL(\cdot \,\|\, \mathbf{q})$. The cost $U$ is the smoothed DAG critical-path length, whose gradient equals path marginals of a Gibbs distribution via forward--backward recursion.For free energy $F_{β_1} = U + β_1^{-1} \DKL(\cdot \,\|\, \mathbf{q})$, we prove well-posedness, monotonic dependence on $β_1$, adaptation bounds via Jeffreys divergence, and a symmetry principle for static optimality. An entropic proximal-gradient method updates multiplicatively with a $|V|$-dim dual KL projection, achieving linear convergence.For time-varying traffic, a threshold policy yields regret $O(\sqrt{ΓC V_1 T})$ against the switching-free optimum. Traffic changes are detected by a multinomial GLR--CUSUM detector with non-asymptotic false-alarm bounds. Multi-job generalized-mean fairness aligns with $α$-fairness ($α\ge 2$). Experiments on pipeline, data, and MoE workloads validate the framework against integer programming.

# gKSM: GPU Memory Deduplication at Driver Layer for Serverless LLM Inference In serverless LLM inference, cloud providers commonly locate multiple instances on a single GPU to improve utilization. However, each instance independently maintains its model weights and runtime state, making duplicate GPU memory the primary bottleneck. Memory deduplication is a widely-used technique for eliminating duplicate data in CPU systems, but extending it to GPU memory faces fundamental challenges. Effective GPU memory deduplication must avoid redundant data movement between CPU and GPU while preserving write isolation for shared pages without native copy-on-write (COW) support.

Effective GPU memory deduplication must avoid redundant data movement between CPU and GPU while preserving write isolation for shared pages without native copy-on-write (COW) support. This paper presents gKSM, a transparent GPU memory deduplication framework for serverless LLM inference. gKSM addresses these challenges through CPU-GPU collaborative hash management that offloads hash computation to GPU kernels, zero-copy model weight deduplication that eliminates duplication before model weight transfer, and a cross-privilege page fault handler that combines a lightweight kernel hook and CUDA Virtual Memory Management (VMM) remapping in the user space. gKSM also designs a stable page scanning algorithm and a reuse-aware placement policy in cluster scale. Experiments show that gKSM reduces GPU memory usage by 59.8% while maintaining high throughput compared to ServerlessLLM. Under memory constrained workloads, gKSM improves aggregate throughput by 2.15X and supports five instances concurrently. In cluster level simulation, gKSM achieves a service rate of 99.97%, compared to 78.2% for SLInfer and 26.9% for ServerlessLLM.

# DROD: Dual-Ratio Ordered Dropout for Federated Continual Learning on Heterogeneous Devices Federated learning for capacity-heterogeneous clients and federated continual learning are each well studied on their own, but their intersection -- clients holding differently sized models while every client's data stream also drifts over time -- remains underexplored. We study this setting directly, training a ResNet-18 fleet from scratch on Split-CIFAR-100 (10 tasks, class-incremental), and introduce DROD (Dual-Ratio Ordered Dropout), which builds on FjORD's Ordered Dropout by using two independent reduction axes to extract sub-models: a shortcut ratio and a branch ratio. On a shared parameter/FLOP budget ladder, DROD achieves the highest mean accuracy among the heterogeneous-model federated learning strategies we compare. Its advantage over the two strongest baseline geometries persists across every replay-buffer size we test and under ER, DER++, and BiC; under EWC, all three geometries collapse alike.

# AgentLens: Framework-Aware Characterization and Resource Control for Heterogeneous LLM Agents LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed on shared hosts, yet their host-side resource demands remain poorly understood, limiting effective resource coordination. We present AgentLens, which combines a cross-framework workload characterization with a framework-aware resource controller for co-located agents. Across 10 frameworks and 11 matched coding tasks, we find that framework orchestration strongly shapes resource demand: framework identity explains 52.95% of peak RSS variance, compared with 4.22% for task identity, while execve events per tool call differ by 39x between MetaGPT and CAMEL. Resource dimensions are not interchangeable: peak RSS and subprocess count have a Spearman correlation of 0.13. Static budgets and framework-agnostic policies miss these structural differences and the alternation between API waiting and tool execution. AgentLens combines offline framework fingerprints with online execution-phase signals to coordinate memory through cgroup v2, without modifying framework internals. In trace-driven replay across three co-location pairs at a memory budget of 90% of aggregate peak demand, AgentLens keeps the protected worker's P95 allocation latency at 5.7-7.1 ms, improving on static allocation by 2.1-2.6x.

# PanoDent-KD: From Generalist Knowledge Distillation to Cross-Dataset Specialist Detection and Embedded Deployment in Panoramic Radiographs Reliable panoramic-radiograph detection requires consistency across datasets with different class definitions and deployment software. We present PanoDent-KD, an auditable 1280-pixel YOLO26m pipeline linking a 12-class source generalist, feature-level knowledge distillation (KD), exact classifier-row transfer, teacher-free five-class specialization, and embedded deployment. A common training and evaluation pipeline compares three source-training arms across three seeds: a supervised baseline (B1), single-teacher KD (STKD), and multi-teacher KD (MTKD). Five shared classifier rows initialize nine OralXrays-9 specialists, while the backbone, FPN-PAN neck, and dual-detection-head topology are retained unchanged. On the 2,686-image test subset, all three arms achieve macro box F1 near 0.82. B1 achieves the highest three-seed arm-level mean macro box F1 (0.8239$\pm$0.0027) and $mAP_{50:95}$ (0.6130$\pm$0.0067). STKD seed 1, selected after development but before final testing, was used for deployment. Its Jetson Orin Nano Super FP16 TensorRT engine achieves 77.03-ms median and 80.86-ms P95 prediction-call latency, throughput of 12.90 images/s, and gross total-module energy of 1.39 J/image, with high numerical agreement between within-device PyTorch and TensorRT FP16 inference. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of an auditable, device-specific deployment workflow, but do not establish clinical validity or improved target-domain accuracy from KD.

# Federated Learning for Malware Image Classification under Data Heterogeneity Malware image classification (MIC), in which binary files are converted into visual representations and deep neural networks are trained to identify malware families, has recently emerged as an effective approach for malware detection. Federated learning (FL) enables malware image classifiers to be trained collaboratively by multiple clients without sharing raw data. However, a fundamental challenge in FL is data heterogeneity (non-IID), which is particularly relevant but understudied in the malware context. In this paper, we address this gap via three contributions. First, we present an empirical study of federated MIC under varying degrees of data heterogeneity across three popular malware image datasets (MalImg, Virus-MNIST, and MalNet). We show that while FL achieves strong accuracy under IID conditions, both accuracy and training stability degrade as data becomes increasingly non-IID.

We show that while FL achieves strong accuracy under IID conditions, both accuracy and training stability degrade as data becomes increasingly non-IID. Second, we introduce a set of round-level statistics that characterize the data contributed by participating clients in each FL round, and demonstrate that class entropy (diversity of class labels present in a given round) exhibits strong positive correlation with global model accuracy. Third, leveraging this insight, we propose an entropy-aware client selection strategy that filters candidate client subsets based on class entropy, and show that our strategy outperforms standard random selection. Our results highlight the role of client composition in federated MIC and underscore the importance of distribution-aware classifier training under data heterogeneity.

# Cryogenic Recharacterization of a Commercial 22 nm FD-SOI Foundry Standard-Cell Library Wiring and bandwidth bottlenecks between a quantum processor and room-temperature electronics can be reduced by placing digital control at the cryogenic stage, but commercial foundry standard-cell libraries are not specified for operation at 4 K. A cryogenic recharacterization flow is therefore developed for a commercial 22 nm FD-SOI foundry standard-cell library using commercially available cryogenic compact-device models, while retaining the original cell circuits, layouts, logic functions, and implementation semantics and remaining compatible with the commercial synthesis, place-and-route, and signoff methodology used at room temperature. Body-bias dependence is quantified over 38,640 matched slew/load points at zero, +/-0.9 V, and +/-1.8 V body bias. Relative to full bias, zero-bias operation increases the median rising and falling delays by 38.6x and 33.0x, while approximately 90% of transitions exceed the foundry-defined maximum-transition envelope.

Relative to full bias, zero-bias operation increases the median rising and falling delays by 38.6x and 33.0x, while approximately 90% of transitions exceed the foundry-defined maximum-transition envelope. The 0.8 V-to-0.4 V level shifter is even more sensitive to body bias: its worst-case falling delay decreases from 30.6 ns at zero bias to 0.56 ns at +/-1.8 V. For the outbound 0.4 V-to-0.8 V crossing, driving the 0.8 V receiver without a level shifter dissipates 57.7 uW of static power per bit at full bias, against 0.196 nW when level-shifted. In post-route analysis of the unchanged extracted physical database of a fabricated 32-bit ALU, the register-to-register setup boundary increases from 1.3 MHz at zero bias to 37.9 MHz at +/-0.9 V and 132.9 MHz at +/-1.8 V.

# ATEST: Adaptive Resource-Aware Test-Time Scaling for LLM Inference Test-time scaling (TTS) improves large language model (LLM) reasoning by sampling multiple answers, but fixed sampling budgets ignore both query difficulty and the changing energy cost of inference under GPU contention. We measure up to a 4.1-fold increase in energy for the same four-sample query as GPU load rises. We present ATEST, a resource-aware TTS framework that jointly considers the expected value of additional samples and their current GPU cost. ATEST-Online, its default mode, requires no offline calibration: it incrementally generates samples, estimates the stability of the plurality answer, monitors live GPU conditions, and learns step energy cost online to decide when to stop. ATEST-Calibrated instead selects a per-query budget using offline accuracy and cost models, favoring deployments with stable loads. We evaluate both modes on four reasoning and question-answering datasets using Phi-3-mini on an NVIDIA A100 under controlled varying load, and test transfer to an NVIDIA L40S and Qwen2.5-3B.

We evaluate both modes on four reasoning and question-answering datasets using Phi-3-mini on an NVIDIA A100 under controlled varying load, and test transfer to an NVIDIA L40S and Qwen2.5-3B. Across the four A100 datasets, ATEST-Online answers every query without exceeding the energy budget, while achieving the highest or statistically tied accuracy and reducing sampling as load increases. On GSM8K at high load, it achieves 60.0% accuracy with no deferrals, versus 44.0% accuracy and 42.4% deferrals for ATEST-Calibrated. Ablations show that online cost learning drives adaptation to load. Including offline profiling, ATEST-Online uses 42 times less GPU time and 48 times less energy than ATEST-Calibrated for the evaluated workload. Online control trades higher tail latency and lower throughput on short tasks for robustness under varying load; offline calibration remains competitive under stable conditions.

# Heuristic-Driven Resource Optimization for Decoupled Memory Channels on FPGAs Determining OpenCL channel depths for Decoupled Access-Execute (DAE) architectures in High-Level Synthesis (HLS) is critical for balancing performance and hardware efficiency. Conventional static analysis tools often over-provision these memory channels to ensure performance safety, leading to significant resource stranding. This paper presents an expansion of an LLVM-based static analysis framework, originally proposed for automated DAE generation, by introducing a hardware-aware refinement layer. We identify a counter-intuitive Performance Inversion Paradox linked to baseline memory stalls, where high-stall, grid-based kernels reach peak performance at minimal channel depths and suffer up to a 61% throughput degradation when depths are increased. We propose a Heuristic Refinement Layer that optimizes OpenCL channel depths based on this correlation between baseline stalls and performance saturation. Experimental results demonstrate that our expanded framework successfully identifies the Minimal Peak Performance point across various benchmarks. By avoiding the performance traps of standard over-provisioning, we achieve a 2.52x improvement in Resource Efficiency for an illustrative HotSpot application. This approach maintains peak execution speedup while ensuring the leanest possible hardware profile, outperforming conservative tool-based static predictions.

# Ride, Raise, or Wake: A Theory of Light-Thread Placement on Multi-Tier Processors hones and laptops now mix several kinds of cores, and each kind sits in its own voltage and clock domain. When a light thread arrives, should it run beside heavy threads on a fast cluster that is already awake, or wake a cluster of efficient cores? We answer with three costs. A thread can \emph{ride} an awake domain at the voltage other threads hold, \emph{raise} that voltage for everyone, or \emph{wake} a sleeping domain and pay its fixed power. From these costs follows a simple rule: ride while the thread's demand is below $r^*=Φ/(e_h-e_l)$, the fixed power of the cluster it would wake over the gap in energy per operation; otherwise wake the smallest tier that can serve it. The best tier is not monotone in demand: tiny threads ride high, medium threads wake a low tier, heavy threads go high again. Two common designs err on opposite sides of the rule: grouping a light thread with the heavy threads of its application overpays above the threshold, and an energy model without idle costs overpays below it. In a model with five tiers, grouping costs 80 to 145\% more energy than the rule, and more as tiers are added. Measurements on an Apple M6 anchor the parameters.

# StreamAhead: Real-Time Streaming Video Question Answering via Adaptive Precomputation Real-time streaming video question answering with vision-language models must answer queries that arrive at any time with low latency while sustaining the video-processing rate required by the application. Existing systems construct key-value (KV) caches for the entire video as it arrives, although a query typically uses only a few of the preceding frames as evidence. This highlights a fundamental trade-off: performing more computation as video arrives reduces query-time computation but can increase processing lag, whereas deferring computation can increase the video-processing rate but requires additional query-time computation for retrieved content. We present StreamAhead, an algorithm-system co-design that exploits this trade-off through adaptive precomputation: dynamically controlling how much computation to complete for each video segment before a query arrives. StreamAhead encodes video segments independently and lets each remain at a different representation level, from inexpensive visual features to costly KV caches, completing KV caches only for the retrieved segments when a query arrives.

StreamAhead encodes video segments independently and lets each remain at a different representation level, from inexpensive visual features to costly KV caches, completing KV caches only for the retrieved segments when a query arrives. StreamAhead profiles offline the cost of advancing a segment to each representation level. Its runtime uses these profiles to schedule segment computation concurrently with query execution, pipelining it across heterogeneous CPU and GPU resources while maintaining the required video-processing rate. StreamAhead achieves accuracy competitive with state-of-the-art methods with up to 10.4x lower time-to-first-token (TTFT), and up to 5.9x lower TTFT than state-of-the-art streaming systems. It sustains 30 FPS with P95 TTFT under 0.5 s, and up to 57 FPS with P95 TTFT under 2 s. To our knowledge, StreamAhead is the first real-time streaming video QA system with competitive accuracy, setting a new Pareto frontier between video-processing rate and TTFT.

# Peer-Relative Trust-Guided Update Screening for Robust Semi-Decentralized Federated Learning under Label-Flipping Attacks Trust and reputation mechanisms can reduce the influence of malicious clients in federated learning (FL), but strict update filtering is difficult under non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data because honest local updates may temporarily reduce performance on a shared validation proxy. Building on our earlier trust-based semi-decentralized FL (SDFL) framework, this paper operationalizes the trust signals and introduces peer-relative update screening that combines a robust validation-utility score with direction- and norm-based update quality. The method is evaluated with 50 MNIST clients, 20% persistent label-flip attackers, Dirichlet heterogeneity levels of 0.5 and 0.1, 100 communication rounds, and five paired random seeds. Under moderate heterogeneity, the proposed method reaches 98.37% final accuracy while rejecting 95.82% of malicious updates and retaining 90.30% of benign updates; the final benign and malicious trust distributions are completely separated (KS=1.00). Under severe heterogeneity, it reaches 95.25% accuracy, rejects 88.55% of malicious updates, and retains 76.90% of benign updates (KS=0.96). Trust weighting alone preserves slightly higher utility in the most heterogeneous condition, but accepts all malicious submis-sions. The results therefore distinguish influence mitigation from explicit containment and quantify the utility-selectivity trade-off introduced by screening. The study provides an empirically validated off-chain governance core that can feed blockchain-based audit and incentive layers in SDFL.

# Robust Resource Allocation for STAR-RIS-Assisted ISAC Networks Using Deep Learning In this paper, we focus on investigating the resource allocation in an integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) system assisted by a simultaneously transmitting and reflecting reconfigurable intelligent surface (STAR-RIS). Due to the coupled non-convex nature of the optimization problem, solving the above joint resource optimization problem while guaranteeing superior sensing performance is challenging, especially in dynamic environment. To conquer such challenge, prior iterative optimization algorithms have been presented. However, practical implementations of these prior algorithms face notable computational challenges, e.g., the reliance on accurate global channel information and the assumption of ideal phase shifts. In this context, we propose a model-driven deep learning framework for jointly optimizing the transmit beamforming and waveform in ISAC networks with low-overhead. In addition, we adopt the Cramer-Rao lower bound (CRLB) as the sensing performance metric, and the multi-user interference (MUI) energy as the communication performance metric for performance evaluation.

In addition, we adopt the Cramer-Rao lower bound (CRLB) as the sensing performance metric, and the multi-user interference (MUI) energy as the communication performance metric for performance evaluation. Besides, our framework jointly optimizes the transmit beamforming, waveform and the STAR-RIS reflection/transmission coefficient matrices by minimizing the weighted sum of MUI energy and CRLB. Our study also considers the impact of imperfect channel information, making the research scenario more aligned with real-world applications. Simulation results validate that the proposed framework not only achieves higher sum-rate performance comparable to traditional iterative algorithms but also significantly reduces computational complexity in terms of algorithm execution time, as well as exhibits inherent robustness.

# Learn the Interface, Not the Implementation: Output Representation Dominates Training Regime in LLM-Based RTL Generation Large-language-model register-transfer-level (RTL) generation has concentrated on how to train the model: fine-tuning, continued pre-training, and reinforcement learning from a verifier. We argue this is the second-order question. On a bounded, formally specifiable task of generating single-error-correcting, double-error-detecting (SECDED) ECC memory wrappers, we hold the task, data, and correctness oracle fixed and vary two axes independently: the training regime (seven settings) and the output representation (four levels, from fully expanded flat Verilog to an eight-field configuration expanded by a deterministic generator). Because a reference generator exists, correctness is decided by formal equivalence over a design space of approximately ten million points, rather than sampled from a hand-written testbench. Two results follow. First, representation dominates: every representation close to raw RTL reaches a pass rate of at most 0.17, while the configuration reaches 0.83 with no training at all.

First, representation dominates: every representation close to raw RTL reaches a pass rate of at most 0.17, while the configuration reaches 0.83 with no training at all. Once the model emits the configuration, every training regime achieves a pass rate between 0.89 and 1.00. Second, raw RTL hits a hard output-length limit: a 512-bit design requires 44,237 tokens of flat Verilog compared with just 69 tokens for the configuration. Consequently, raw generation becomes infeasible above 32-bit data words rather than merely inaccurate. A model trained from scratch with fewer than 50 million parameters, combined with the verified generator, achieves 0.89 formal equivalence, compared with 1.00 for a 32-billion-parameter fine-tuned model, while using approximately 1600 times less inference energy per correct design. Inference energy also dominates amortized training energy. The lesson is to learn the interface, not the implementation.

# An Event-Driven System Architecture for a 15-Minute Urban Flood Digital Twin: A Hanoi Case Study Flash floods in Hanoi submerge roads within minutes of heavy rain onset, yet public flood advisories remain retrospective. Hydrodynamic models could supply forward-looking depth guidance, but they are typically run offline for historical events, and prior studies have not evaluated whether physics-based simulation, spatial serving, and vehicle-aware routing can operate together within a fixed refresh cycle using a cloud solver and a single commodity server. This paper evaluates an end-to-end prototype of an automated flood digital twin designed to meet a 15-minute refresh cycle under data scarcity. The architecture organizes execution into decoupled, event-driven workflows that chain weather-gated 3Di simulations through hydraulic restart states, serve flood depths through a dual-track spatial layer, and publish road-edge depths via standardized output contracts.

The architecture organizes execution into decoupled, event-driven workflows that chain weather-gated 3Di simulations through hydraulic restart states, serve flood depths through a dual-track spatial layer, and publish road-edge depths via standardized output contracts. Evaluated on a 57-run storm replay in the My Dinh and Tay Mo sector of Hanoi driven by satellite rainfall estimates, every cycle completed within the 15-minute deadline, publishing a ready edge table at a median of 537 s after slot start. Indexed raster tiles resolved point-depth lookups in a median of 0.54 ms (277 times faster than un-tiled rasters), while pre-rendered vector tiles served web maps without database queries. These findings demonstrate that a commodity server coupled to a cloud solver can sustain the 15-minute operational cycle and decouple routing policies from simulation internals. Because simulated depths were not validated against field gauges and the replay used observed satellite rainfall, the results establish system feasibility rather than forecast accuracy or route safety.

# MX-Like Tensor Core for LLM Inference with NPU Integration via Hardware-Software Co-Design Exploration Block-scaled quantization formats such as OCP Microscaling (MX) and NVFP4 have been widely adopted as efficient data formats for LLM inference. However, the design space of these formats spanned by shared scale, weight, and activation format combinations has not been systematically explored, and the joint accuracy-silicon tradeoff across this space remains uncharacterized, leaving the true Pareto-optimal configurations for NPU-based edge LLM deployment an open question. To bridge this gap, we conduct a joint hardware-software (HW-SW) co-design exploration of the above underexplored MX-like design space with three innovations. 1) We define and systematically characterize the full 8-bit scale format family within the MX-like design space, jointly with asymmetric weight-activation precision, identifying configurations that outperform the MX and NVFP4-like (without per-tensor scaling, PTS) baselines. 2) We build a per-format specialized MAC datapath template that enables fair hardware cost evaluation across the space.

2) We build a per-format specialized MAC datapath template that enables fair hardware cost evaluation across the space. 3) We develop an automated co-design flow, integrated into the open-source SNAX NPU platform, that enables joint HW-SW analysis across the design space. Overall, our co-design exploration reveals that scale format matters only under aggressive FP4 quantization, yielding a case-oriented design guideline for both scale format and asymmetric weight-activation precision. We further identify UE5M3 as a favorable accuracy-hardware tradeoff for the FP4 regime, reducing perplexity degradation by up to 25.3% relative to the NVFP4-like baseline, at a cost of only +0.06% area and +0.49% power overhead.

# Superposed analog memory for vector storage in neural networks The growing memory demands of artificial neural networks pose a major challenge for energy-efficient computing, particularly for models that rely on large collections of high-dimensional weight and embedding vectors. Conventional memory architectures store these vectors individually, requiring many memory cells per vector and limiting achievable storage density. Here we demonstrate an analog memory architecture that encodes multiple vectors in a distributed superposition within a single memory array. Individual vectors are recovered through in-memory matrix-vector multiplication, allowing the degree of superposition to be tuned to balance storage density against recall fidelity. This approach introduces a new scaling dimension for analog memory, in which effective storage density can be increased without a corresponding increase in the number of physical memory cells. The distributed representation also provides resilience to device-level noise. We implement the architecture on a prototype phase-change memory chip and experimentally evaluate it using embedding tables from deep learning recommendation models and large language models. The results demonstrate inference accuracy comparable to full-precision software baselines, establishing analog superposition as a promising route towards dense, energy-efficient memory for artificial intelligence.

# A Hybrid GPU and Processing-Near-Memory Architecture with Shared DRAM for Efficient Prefill-Decode Disaggregation The growing adoption of large language models (LLMs) has significantly increased the compute and memory demands of inference serving. A key challenge arises from the mismatch between compute-bound prefill and memory-bound decoding: when executed together, the two phases interfere, while separating them via prefill-decode (PD) disaggregation leads to substantial resource underutilization. Specifically, prefill leaves memory bandwidth underutilized, whereas decoding underutilizes compute resources. Prior approaches, such as GPU Streaming Multiprocessor (SM) partitioning, attempt to improve utilization by spatially dividing GPU resources. However, these approaches remain fundamentally limited, as memory-bound decoding still requires a large number of SMs to saturate bandwidth, reducing the compute resources available for prefill and resulting in an inherent trade-off. To address this limitation, we propose DuoPD, a hybrid PD-disaggregation architecture that integrates lightweight Processing-Near-Memory (PNM) units into the HBM logic die.

To address this limitation, we propose DuoPD, a hybrid PD-disaggregation architecture that integrates lightweight Processing-Near-Memory (PNM) units into the HBM logic die. Unlike prior PIM/PNM designs that rely on costly internal bandwidth scaling and offload only partial decoding operations, DuoPD enables full decoding execution on PNM by leveraging bandwidth sharing with the GPU over a shared HBM interface. This allows compute-bound prefill and memory-bound decoding to execute concurrently with minimal interference, improving both compute and memory utilization. To realize this design, we develop a compact PNM microarchitecture, a TSV-level bandwidth sharing mechanism, and a hierarchical data mapping scheme tailored for hybrid GPU-PNM execution. Evaluations on server-scale LLMs demonstrate that DuoPD achieves up to 2.23x higher end-to-end throughput than conventional PD-disaggregation.

# Fault-Tolerant Offloading Framework for Real-Time Applications in Mobile Edge Computing This paper studies a Deadline-constrained task Offloading and resource Allocation Problem (DOAP) in a backhaul-network-enabled Mobile Edge Computing (MEC) system with both bandwidth and computational resource constraints. The goal is to maximize the total inference accuracy improvement across all tasks. We formulate this problem, denoted as $\mathbf{P}$, as an Integer Linear Programming (ILP) problem and show it is NP-hard via a reduction from the maximum-weight three-dimensional matching problem. To address $\mathbf{P}$, we develop $\mathtt{FastSA}$, a linear-time $\frac{1}{10}$-approximation algorithm based on the local-ratio technique. To the best of our knowledge, $\mathtt{FastSA}$ provides the first constant-factor performance guarantee for backhaul-network-enabled DOAPs. In addition, we introduce a fault detection and recovery framework that enables robust MEC operation under backhaul link and edge server failures. Experiments using profiled image classification workloads and real-world taxi traces show that $\mathtt{FastSA}$ achieves an average accuracy improvement of $25.6\%$ over benchmark algorithms under fault-free conditions while maintaining the lowest runtime. Under fault-injected scenarios, our framework reduces performance degradation by an average of $12.8\%$, demonstrating its effectiveness in fault handling.

# Holistic Buoyancy-Driven Cloud Native Resource Management Efficient resource management is a challenge in multi-tenant cloud environments as workloads compete for shared resources such as last-level cache and memory bandwidth, whose congestion can change dynamically as workload composition and resource demands evolve. Existing resource management approaches often rely on static resource requirements or prior workload profiling, limiting their ability to respond to changing resource contention as required in the cloud. In this paper, we leverage workload buoyancy, a runtime framework for capturing workload sensitivity to individual resources and application-level performance, to enable adaptive scheduling and resource management. We propose a holistic approach that incorporates buoyancy into workload scheduling, node-local resource allocation, and workload rescheduling throughout the workload lifecycle. We implement our approach as a Kubernetes-native prototype and evaluate it on a multi-node cluster using diverse cloud workloads under varying levels of resource contention. In a high-congestion scenario, our approach increases the percentage of workloads satisfying their SLOs from 7.74% to 87.8% on average compared with the Kubernetes baseline, while reducing resource congestion, the severity of SLO violations, and cluster fragmentation using limited rescheduling.

# CEMA-Router: Infrastructure-Aware Batch Routing for LLM Inference in Cloud-Edge Systems Large language models (LLM) are increasingly integrated into pervasive applications spanning heterogeneous cloud-edge resources. These heterogeneous resources differ in computational capacity, energy efficiency, network conditions, and deployed model quality, creating trade-offs among response quality, monetary cost, energy consumption, and batch completion time when routing inference requests.
